Before diving into all its meanings, it helps to know what ties them together. A note is always something brief, distinct, and pointed — whether it's a piece of writing, a sound, a quality you sense, or a mark of importance. Every meaning of this word carries the idea of something small but significant, something that stands out or is worth paying attention to.
Meaning 1: A Short Piece of Writing

This is the meaning most people think of first. A note is a brief written message or record — something short and informal, not a full letter or a long document.

  • You write a note on a piece of paper and stick it to the fridge: "Gone to the market. Back by 7."
  • A student passes a note to a friend in class.
  • You jot down a quick note on your phone so you don't forget something.

The key quality here is brevity. A note is not meant to be long. It captures the essential point quickly. If you sit down and write three full pages to someone, that's a letter. If you scribble a few lines, that's a note.

Within this meaning, there are a few flavours worth knowing:

A personal note is a short, informal message written to someone you know — a thank-you note, a note of apology, a note left on someone's desk.

A note to yourself (also called a reminder note) is something you write so you remember something — a shopping list item, an idea, a phone number.

Notes (in the plural) refers to information you write down while listening to someone or reading something, so you can refer to it later. Students take notes during class. Journalists take notes during interviews. "I made notes during the lecture." These notes are a way of capturing something so it isn't lost.
Meaning 2: A Short Explanatory Comment Added to a Text

When you read a book, an article, or an official document, you sometimes see small additional explanations added alongside the main text. These are called notes.

  • A footnote is a note placed at the bottom of a page to explain a word, add extra information, or cite a source.
  • An endnote is the same kind of thing, but placed at the end of a book or chapter.
  • An editor's note is a comment added by someone who prepared the text for publishing, giving the reader useful context.

"See note 3 for a full explanation of this term."

These notes are not part of the main flow of the writing — they exist alongside it to help the reader understand something better. They are brief by nature.
Meaning 3: A Formal or Official Written Communication

In more formal or official contexts — especially in diplomacy, business, or law — a note is a written document sent from one party to another to communicate something officially.

  • Governments send each other diplomatic notes — formal written communications between countries on matters of policy.
  • "The embassy sent a strongly worded note to the foreign ministry."
  • In older legal and business language, a promissory note (often just called a note) is a written promise to pay a specific amount of money to someone by a specific date. It is a legally binding document.

Here the word has a more serious, official weight, but the core idea is the same — a written communication that conveys something concisely and on the record.
Meaning 4: A Banknote (Paper Money)

In British English especially, and widely across the world, a note is a piece of paper money — what Americans call a bill.

  • "Can you give me change? I only have a fifty-pound note."
  • "She took out a crisp hundred-rupee note from her wallet."
  • "He counted out five notes and handed them over."

A note in this sense is a physical piece of currency. It is sometimes called a banknote to be precise. Coins are not notes — notes are specifically paper currency.
Meaning 5: A Single Musical Sound

In music, a note is one individual sound of a specific pitch — the basic unit of music.

  • When a pianist presses a single key, that produces one note.
  • "She played the wrong note."
  • "The song begins with a long, held note."

A musical note has two things that define it: its pitch (how high or low the sound is — like the difference between a squeak and a rumble) and its duration (how long it lasts).

Notes also exist as written symbols on a sheet of music — the little oval shapes sitting on lines and spaces that tell a musician what sound to produce and for how long. So a "note" can refer either to the sound itself or the written symbol representing that sound.

The notes in the Western musical system have names: C, D, E, F, G, A, B — and these repeat at higher and lower pitches.

"She hit every note perfectly in the performance." Here, "hit a note" means to produce the correct pitch at the right moment.
Meaning 6: A Particular Quality, Tone, or Feeling

This is a more figurative meaning, but it is extremely common in everyday English. A note can refer to a particular quality, feeling, or mood that you sense in something — in a person's voice, in the atmosphere of a situation, in the way something is written, or even in a smell or flavour.

  • "There was a note of sadness in her voice." — Her voice had a quality that told you she was a little sad.
  • "He ended his speech on a hopeful note." — The feeling or tone at the end of his speech was hopeful.
  • "I detected a note of sarcasm in his reply." — I sensed sarcasm in how he said it.
  • "The perfume has a note of jasmine." — One of the distinct smells you can detect in it is jasmine.
  • "The evening ended on a sour note." — Things became unpleasant by the end.

This usage comes from music, where a single note creates a particular mood or feeling. When applied to life and language, a "note" captures that subtle, distinct quality that colours a situation.

Phrases like "on a high note" (ending something in a positive or successful way), "on a low note" (ending something badly or disappointingly), and "on a serious note" (shifting the tone to something more grave) all use this musical-emotional idea of a note.
Meaning 7: Importance, Distinction, or Worth Noticing

A note can also refer to significance — the quality of being important or worth attention. This meaning is less about something you write or hear, and more about status or worthiness.

  • "Nothing of note happened today." — Nothing significant or worth mentioning happened.
  • "She is a writer of note." — She is a notable, distinguished, well-regarded writer.
  • "He is a scholar of some note." — He has a certain reputation and importance in his field.
  • "The meeting produced nothing of note." — The meeting produced no results worth paying attention to.

Here, a person or thing "of note" is one that stands out — one that deserves to be noticed and remembered.
Important Phrases and Expressions Built Around "Note"

Since you want to know everything about this word, here are the key fixed expressions that use "note" as a noun:

Take note (or take note of something): To pay careful attention to something; to consciously register it.
"Take note of the emergency exit locations." — Notice them, remember them.

Of note: Significant, worth mentioning.
"There were no problems of note."

On a [adjective] note: With a particular quality or feeling at a certain point, especially at the beginning or end of something.
"Let's end on a positive note." / "On a more personal note, I'd like to thank my family."

A note of [something]: A detectable trace of a quality or emotion.
"There was a note of desperation in his request."

Compare notes: When two or more people share and discuss their observations, information, or experiences about the same thing.
"After the meeting, we compared notes to see if we had noticed the same things."

Strike a note (or strike the right/wrong note): To create a particular impression or feeling — correctly or incorrectly suited to a situation.
"His apology struck the right note — it felt sincere." / "Her jokes struck a wrong note at the funeral."

Worthy of note: Deserving attention; significant enough to be mentioned.
"One fact worthy of note is that the building was never finished."
How All These Meanings Fit Together

You might wonder: what do music, paper money, short messages, and feelings have to do with each other?

The thread is this: a note is always something brief, distinct, and meaningful that stands out. A musical note is one clear, distinct sound. A written note is a short, focused message. A note of sadness is a distinct quality that you can detect. A person of note is someone who stands out in their field. A banknote is a distinct, recognized unit of value.

Each meaning takes this same core idea — something precise and noticeable — and applies it to a different domain of life.
A Quick Summary of All the Meanings

• A short written message or record (a note on the fridge; taking notes in class)
  • A brief explanatory comment added to a text (footnotes; editor's notes)
  • A formal written communication (a diplomatic note; a promissory note)
  • Paper money (a ten-pound note)
  • A single musical sound of a specific pitch (playing a note on the piano)
  • A quality or tone that you sense in a voice, atmosphere, smell, or flavour (a note of bitterness; on a high note)
  • Importance or distinction (nothing of note; a scientist of note)
